title: st.slider corrupts min_value/max_value when bounds are reversed, silently producing a wrong range
body:
### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar issues.
- [x] I added a very descriptive title to this issue.
- [x] I have provided sufficient information below to help reproduce this issue.

### Summary

`_slider()` tries to swap reversed bounds with two sequential statements, but the second one reads the variable the first one just overwrote:

```python
# lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/slider.py:1081-1083
# Ensure that min <= value(s) <= max, adjusting the bounds as necessary.
min_value = min(min_value, max_value)
max_value = max(min_value, max_value)   # <-- min_value is already the new (smaller) value
```

After line 1082, `min_value` is `min(a, b)`, so line 1083 evaluates `max(min(a, b), b)`, which is always `b`. The original `min_value` can never become the upper bound, so the intended swap never happens. Depending on what `value` is, this silently produces a wrong range or raises an exception quoting numbers the user never passed.

### Reproducible Code Example

```python
import streamlit as st

# 1. Bounds silently reinterpreted
st.slider("a", 10, 1)                                  # -> range 1..10, value 10

# 2. Upper bound silently invented from `value`
st.slider("b", min_value=10, max_value=1, value=5)     # -> range 1..5  (max_value=1 is gone)

# 3. Spurious exception quoting numbers the user never passed
st.slider("c", min_value=10, max_value=1, value=1)     # -> StreamlitAPIException
```

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Run any of the three lines above.
2. Compare the resulting slider bounds against the arguments passed.

### Expected Behavior

Either of the following would be self-consistent:

- Reject reversed bounds with a clear error naming the two values the caller actually supplied, the way `st.date_input` already does:
  > The `min_value`, set to 2024-01-02, shouldn't be larger than the `max_value`, set to 2024-01-01.
- Or genuinely swap them, so `st.slider("a", 10, 1)` yields a `1..10` slider — which is what the code comment says it intends.

Today it does neither reliably.

### Current Behavior

Verified with `streamlit.testing.v1.AppTest`:

```
slider(min=10, max=1)            -> min=1.0 max=10.0 value=10
slider(min=10, max=1, value=5)   -> min=1.0 max=5.0  value=5
slider(min=10, max=1, value=1)   -> RAISED: Slider `min_value` must be less than the `max_value`.
                                            The values were 1 and 1.
```

Note case 3: the user passed `10` and `1`, but the error reports "The values were 1 and 1" — both numbers have been overwritten by the faulty normalization. Case 2 is the most damaging, because it silently produces a slider whose upper bound (`5`) was never supplied as a bound at all; it leaked in from `value`.

Isolating just the two lines:

```python
min_value, max_value = 10, 1
min_value = min(min_value, max_value)
max_value = max(min_value, max_value)
print(min_value, max_value)   # 1 1     <-- current behavior

min_value, max_value = 10, 1
min_value, max_value = min(min_value, max_value), max(min_value, max_value)
print(min_value, max_value)   # 1 10    <-- intended
```

The `min_value == max_value` guard at line 1137 then fires on values that are an artifact of this bug rather than of user input, and it only catches the case where the corruption happens to collapse both bounds to the same number — which is why `st.slider("x", 5, 5)` errors while `st.slider("x", 10, 1)` does not.

### Suggested Fix

Assign both bounds simultaneously (or compute the max from the original value):

```python
min_value, max_value = min(min_value, max_value), max(min_value, max_value)
```

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `st.slider("b", min_value=10, max_value=1, value=5)` no longer produces a slider whose upper bound came from `value`.
- [ ] Reversed bounds either swap correctly or raise an error that quotes the values the caller actually passed.
- [ ] Test coverage for reversed `min_value`/`max_value` with `value` below, inside, and above the range.

### Is this a regression?

- [ ] Yes, this used to work in a previous version.

Unknown.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.62.0 (`develop`, commit `2ac0d77d3`)
- Python version: 3.13.6
- Operating System: Windows 11 (logic is platform-independent)
- Browser: n/a (reproduced headlessly via `streamlit.testing.v1.AppTest`)

### Additional Information

Related but distinct: #5099 covers `value` falling outside `(min_value, max_value)`. This report is specifically about the bound-normalization statements corrupting `min_value`/`max_value` themselves.

comments.body:
I have a fix with tests ready, but this repository limits opening pull requests to collaborators, so I can't submit it as a PR. Posting the patch here in case a maintainer wants to pick it up.

Branch: https://github.com/rajarshidattapy/streamlit/tree/fix/slider-reversed-bounds-normalization

The library change assigns both bounds at once, so the swap reads the original `min_value`:

```diff
 # Ensure that min <= value(s) <= max, adjusting the bounds as necessary.
-min_value = min(min_value, max_value)
-max_value = max(min_value, max_value)
+# Assign both at once so the swap reads the original min_value; assigning
+# min_value first would leave max_value unable to take the original min.
+min_value, max_value = min(min_value, max_value), max(min_value, max_value)
```

I went with completing the swap rather than raising on reversed bounds, since that is what the existing comment ("adjusting the bounds as necessary") and the neighbouring `start > end` swap already intend. Rejecting reversed bounds instead would be a behaviour change worth deciding separately.

Added to `lib/tests/streamlit/elements/slider_test.py`:

- `test_reversed_bounds_are_swapped` — parameterized over `value` omitted / at min / inside range / at max, asserting `c.min == 1` and `c.max == 10` in every case. The `value_inside_range` case is the one that previously produced a `1..5` slider, with the upper bound leaking in from `value`.
- `test_reversed_bounds_do_not_collapse_to_equal_values` — covers the float case that previously raised `Slider min_value must be less than the max_value. The values were 1 and 1`.

Behaviour before and after, via `AppTest` (Python 3.13.6, `develop` @ `2ac0d77d3`):

| call | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `st.slider("a", 10, 1)` | `min=1 max=10 value=10` | `min=1 max=10 value=10` |
| `st.slider("b", min_value=10, max_value=1, value=5)` | `min=1 max=5 value=5` | `min=1 max=10 value=5` |
| `st.slider("c", min_value=10, max_value=1, value=1)` | raised `The values were 1 and 1` | `min=1 max=10 value=1` |

The existing `test_max_min` and `test_min_equals_max` still pass, so equal bounds are still rejected and the previously-passing reversed case is unchanged.

This is a real backend bug in `_slider()` bound normalization, not a frontend or widget-state issue. In `lib/streamlit/elements/widgets/slider.py`, reversed bounds are meant to be swapped (`min_value = min(...)` then `max_value = max(...)`), but the second assignment reads the already-overwritten `min_value`, so `max_value` always collapses to the original `max_value`. After that, the existing “expand bounds to include `value`” logic can invent an upper bound from `value` (`min_value=10, max_value=1, value=5` → range `1..5`) or make both bounds equal and raise `The values were 1 and 1` for inputs the user never passed. Existing `test_max_min` only covers the case where `value` equals the original min, which accidentally restores the lost bound, so the tests never caught this. A simultaneous swap (`min_value, max_value = min(...), max(...)`) matches the current comment and the range-handle swap a few lines below; alternatively, `st.date_input` / `st.datetime_input` already reject reversed bounds with the original values quoted. The reporter also posted a ready-to-apply patch in the issue thread.

### Related Issues

- [#5099](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/5099) — Confirmed `st.slider` behavior of expanding `min_value`/`max_value` to include an out-of-range `value`. Distinct from this report (which is about the failed bound swap itself), but it is the neighboring code path that turns the corrupted bounds into a silently wrong range.

No duplicate of this reversed-bounds assignment bug was found among open issues.
